author: Rimbaud
title: The experiment and its record
where: *A Season in Hell* (*Une saison en enfer*, 1873): the chapters “Alchemy of the Word” and “Adieu”
about: Rimbaud dated this short prose book April to August 1873, when he was eighteen. A first-person speaker gives what he calls the account of his hell. In the chapter “Alchemy of the Word” he tells the story of one of his follies, his attempt to invent a new language for poetry, and quotes seven of his own poems; “Adieu” is the last chapter. The French is that of the first edition, and the English beside it was printed, unsigned, in *The Dial* in 1920.

view.says: Auden writes that the Romantic artist becomes his own hero. He makes the experiment on himself and keeps the record, and a catastrophe drives him to the point of exhaustion. Rimbaud’s account of himself in the first passage below holds to some degree, Auden says, for every Romantic artist. Some came to see that the artist is no religious hero, only a man exploring what is possible.
view.quote: The artist who has thus to be at once the subject of his experiment and the recorder enjoys excitement and suffers terrors hardly known before.
view.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), chapter 3, pp. 147–49

plates.heading: “Alchemy of the Word”: what he saw

lenses.caption: The French here tells the past in two tenses. In a school grammar of the time the past definite shows a thing done in a time completely over, the imperfect a thing going on at a past time. Three steps are in the past definite: Je m’habituai, I got used; Puis j’expliquai, then I explained; Je finis par, I ended by. What he saw, was and envied is in the imperfect. The Dial marks the difference once, in used to see. So each step is told as done and over; the chapter’s first line announces the story of one of his follies.
lenses.why: The steps stand in the past definite, which the grammar of the time keeps for a time completely over: he sets down as closed history what he did to himself.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages. Noël and Chapsal’s *Nouvelle grammaire française* (1863), nos. 118 and 481, for what the two tenses tell. The [first line of the chapter](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:0).

lenses.label: List
lenses.name: asyndeton
lenses.plain: phrases set side by side with no joining word between them
lenses.caption: After je voyais, I saw, come four things and then two nouns alone, with no et, the French for and, to join them. This is asyndeton; Littré’s dictionary says the joining words are dropped to gain speed. The first thing is set against what was there: the mosque stands à la place d’une usine, in place of a factory. The next three have no such anchor: a drum school made by angels, carriages on sky roads, a drawing room at a lake’s bottom. Nothing is said to be like anything; the verb is plain seeing. In the last clause a play’s title raises épouvantes, terrors.
lenses.why: With the joining words dropped, six things seen follow one verb at speed, and after the first none is set against anything real; then a play’s title raises terrors.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages, and what the sentence says. Littré’s *Dictionnaire de la langue française* under *asyndète*, *disjonction*, *salon*, *calèche*, *vaudeville* and *épouvante*.

lenses.label: Judgment

notes.note: Littré gives both senses; the Dial puts *quite frankly* in front of the verb, where it can be read as a remark on the telling.
Littré: said of things that deserve to be venerated and never violated; the Dial has *holy*.
Littré has the phrase itself, *disorder of mind*: the state of a mind ill regulated. Its first sense is want of order, confusion; the Dial has *confusion*.
Littré: one who is doing nothing at present; the Dial has *lazy*.

lenses.caption: In each paragraph a noun names what he tells of. Hallucination is in Littré’s dictionary a term of medicine: sensations that no outside object causes. A sophisme is a false reasoning that looks true. Désordre of mind is the state of a mind ill regulated. In each paragraph a second word is marked. He saw très-franchement, sincerely, or without hesitating. The sophisms are magiques, of magic. The disorder he ended by finding sacré, worthy of veneration. The chapter’s first line calls this one of his follies; later he says he has forgotten none of the sophisms of madness.
lenses.why: He names what he tells of in words for something gone wrong: a medical term, false reasoning, a mind ill regulated. Yet he saw frankly and found the disorder sacred. The chapter calls the story one of his follies.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *hallucination*, *sophisme*, *désordre*, *franchement*, *magique* and *sacré*. The [first line of the chapter](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:0), and what he says [later in it](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:46) about the sophisms of madness.

lenses.label: Innocence

notes.note: Littré: the state of one who enjoys what contents him; the Dial has *contentment*.
One of Littré’s senses of the verb; the Dial has *symbolize*.
Littré: the theologians’ word for the place where the just of the Old Testament waited for Christ; some put there the children who died unbaptized; it is pictured at the edge of hell.
Littré: their eyes are so small and so hidden that people long denied they had any; to be underground like a mole is to live hidden.

lenses.caption: The last sentence says what he envied: the félicité, the contented state, of bêtes, beasts. In Littré’s dictionary a bête is any animal except man, and the entry’s first example says the beast lacks reason. Caterpillars are the image of the innocence of limbes, limbo: in Littré, the place at the edge of hell where some theologians put children who died unbaptized. Moles are the sleep of virginity. In “Night in Hell” the speaker calls himself the slave of his baptism. Shortly before quoting these lines, Auden speaks of the Romantics’ identifying sin with consciousness, and asks whether such longing for innocence is not the mark of the explorer of the unknown.
lenses.why: He envies creatures without reason and names limbo, where some put the unbaptized, in a book whose speaker calls himself the slave of his baptism. Auden ties the Romantic identification of sin with consciousness to the explorer’s longing for innocence.
lenses.stands: What the sentence says. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *félicité*, *bête*, *chenille*, *représenter*, *limbes* and *taupe*. [“Night in Hell”](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s3:3), for the slave of his baptism. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 146–47.

plates.heading: “Alchemy of the Word”: a stanza of his own, and the sentence before it
plates.label: Rimbaud, 1873

lenses.label: Count
lenses.meterName: five counted syllables, the accent on the last; the fourth line has three
lenses.caption: French verse counts syllables, and its fixed accent falls on the last sounded syllable of the line. Auden says an English ear finds verse measured by syllables very hard to grasp. Three lines here count five. The fourth stops at three: Au soleil, with the sun. In the next three stanzas of the poem the fourth line counts five, and printed on its own in 1886 the poem has five syllables in this line too. Earlier in the chapter Rimbaud says he prided himself on inventing a poetic language with instinctive rhythms; this poem is one of the seven he gives.
lenses.why: The last line drops from five syllables to three, where the next three stanzas, and this one as printed in 1886, keep five. In this chapter he says he prided himself on inventing a poetic language with instinctive rhythms.

points.say: The mute *e* of *Elle* runs into *est* and is not counted, so the line has five syllables.
A question of one word. It can be heard with its own stress and a pause after it.

Five syllables again. Lines of five are mostly mixed with longer ones. A history of French verse finds whole stanzas of them now and then in Old French pastourelles and romances, and less rarely in Rimbaud’s century, in Banville, Richepin and Verlaine.
A mute *e* at the end of a line is never counted.
Three syllables, where each line above has five.

lenses.stands: The marks on the stanza, and a count of [the stanzas that follow it](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:39). L. E. Kastner, *A History of French Versification* (1903): chapters 1 and 2 for how a line is counted, chapter 8 for the five-syllable line. The poem as printed in *Les Illuminations* (1886), pp. 85–86. Rimbaud on [his instinctive rhythms](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:4), and Auden in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 297.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Three of the four lines end on one sound, é: retrouvée, found again; éternité, eternity; mêlée, mixed. By the rules of French verse only the first and third can rhyme together. They end in a silent e, which French calls a feminine ending; éternité does not. A history of French verse says the rules forbid rhyming the two kinds together even where they sound alike, and that a few modern poets break the rule. So the ear joins three lines where the rule joins two. The last line, soleil, sun, has no partner. Early in the chapter Rimbaud lists silly refrains and naive rhythms among the things he loved.
lenses.why: One sound ends three lines though the rule lets only two of them rhyme: the stanza rhymes by ear where the rule forbids it, and Rimbaud says in this chapter that he loved naive rhythms.
lenses.stands: The marks on the stanza. Kastner, *A History of French Versification*, chapter 3, on masculine and feminine rhyme. Rimbaud’s [list of what he loved](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:2), in the Dial’s words.

lenses.label: Frame

notes.note: The verb is in the imperfect, the tense of what was going on; the Dial has *began to wear*.
Littré gives both: the way of putting a thought into speech or writing, and the way feelings show in the features.
Littré: of the *bouffon*, the stage character whose part is to raise a laugh; said of writing, the low comic.
Littré: one who has lost his way; also said of eyes or a bearing that show a mind astray.
The French sentence ends on a colon, and the poem follows; the Dial ends its sentence on a full stop.
*Elle*, she, stands for the feminine noun of the next line; Littré gives *retrouver* as to find again, and to find a thing that had been lost.

lenses.caption: The Dial leaves the poems of this chapter in French. This stanza says that eternity is found again and is the sea mixed with the sun. The sentence before it says that for joy he took on an expression that was bouffonne and égarée to the last degree. In Littré’s dictionary a bouffon is the stage character who raises a laugh, and égaré is said of a look that shows a mind astray. Expression is the look on a face, as the Dial takes it, and also the wording of a thought. The sentence ends on a colon, which a school grammar of the time says announces a quotation, and the stanza follows.
lenses.why: The sentence before the stanza calls his expression clownish and astray to the last degree, and expression means both a look and a wording. It stops on a colon, the mark that announces a quotation, and his stanza follows.
lenses.stands: What the stanza and the sentence before it say, with Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *expression*, *bouffon*, *égaré*, *possible*, *retrouver* and *mêlé*. Noël and Chapsal’s *Nouvelle grammaire française* (1863), nos. 670 to 672, on the colon. The Dial’s English of [the chapter](#/read/rimbaud/s5:36), which leaves the poems in French. The punctuation of the two sentences as printed here.

lenses.label: Chapter
lenses.what: how the seven poems stand in the prose of “Alchemy of the Word”

facts.says: the story of one of his follies; at first it was a study

facts.here: three of its paragraphs are the first passage
its last sentence is the sentence of this passage
its first stanza is the stanza of this passage, and comes back as its last

facts.says: none of the sophisms of madness forgotten
that is over; today he knows how to greet beauty

lenses.caption: As printed here the chapter has 663 words of prose in 23 paragraphs and 518 of verse: seven of his own poems, 113 lines. The first line announces the story of one of his follies. At first, he says, it was une étude, a study. The prose tells it mostly in past tenses; three times it stops on a colon and a poem follows. The last line says this is over; today he knows how to greet beauty. The Dial’s translator says the poems are quoted as examples of the new poetic language Rimbaud thought he had made.
lenses.why: Seven of his own poems stand in prose that tells in past tenses what he did and ends by saying it is over. The Dial’s translator calls them examples of a new poetic language.
lenses.stands: A count of the chapter in the French text printed here: a word is whatever stands between two spaces, so two words joined by a dash with no space count as one; paragraphs and lines are as that text sets them. The [first](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:0) and [last](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:58) lines of the chapter, and [the sentence that calls the work a study](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s5:5). The translator’s note in *The Dial*, July 1920, p. 2.

plates.heading: “Adieu”: the end of the fourth paragraph, the fifth, and the seventh
plates.label: Rimbaud, 1873

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word at the head of sentence after sentence, or of phrase after phrase
lenses.caption: Three sentences begin J’ai, I have. This is anaphora, one word set at the head of each sentence. Inside them the repeating goes on: all three times, new four times. What he claims goes from feasts, triumphs and dramas to new flowers, stars, flesh and tongues, and then to supernatural powers. Set side by side, the verbs claim less each time: he has created, he has tried to invent, he has believed that he was gaining. The next sentence begins Eh bien!, well, and says he must bury his imagination.
lenses.why: Three claims in one form stand side by side, and their verbs weaken: created, tried, believed. In the next sentence he must bury his imagination.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages, and what the sentences say. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *anaphore*.

lenses.label: Time
lenses.caption: The main verbs go from past to present to future. The three claims stand in the past indefinite, J’ai with a participle: I have created, tried, believed. A school grammar of the day says this tense can be used of a time not yet over, where the past definite of the first passage is kept for a time completely past. Then the present: je dois, I must, and je suis rendu, I am given back. Then the future: je demanderai, I shall ask. The last verb is a command in the form for we: allons, let us go. Auden says this book is where Rimbaud spoke of himself before he took leave of art.
lenses.why: The claims stand in the past indefinite, which the grammar lets reach to the present; then come must, am, shall and a last let us go: the passage turns from what he has done to what is to do.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages. Noël and Chapsal’s *Nouvelle grammaire française* (1863), nos. 118, 480 and 481, on the past tenses. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *aller*, for *allons*. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 148.

lenses.label: Sentence

spans.label: the Dial: free from every rule

lenses.caption: The middle paragraph is one sentence and one word. It begins Moi! moi, I, I, and before any main verb says he called himself magus or angel and was excused from all morality. The main clause comes at the fourteenth word, with a passive verb: je suis rendu au sol, I am given back to the ground. He did the naming; the giving back is done to him. Two things remain to do: a duty to look for, a rough reality to clasp. Then Paysan!, peasant. In “Bad Blood” masters and workmen alike are peasants, ignoble. Auden quotes this paragraph for the artist who finds he is no religious hero.
lenses.why: The sentence Auden quotes says the old titles first and keeps its main verb for what has happened to him, and that verb is passive: he called himself magus or angel; he is given back to the ground.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages, and what the sentence says. [“Bad Blood”](#/read/rimbaud-fr/s2:3), for the peasants. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *rendu* and *paysan*. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 149–50.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Littré gives *mage* three senses: a priest of ancient Persia, one of the three Magi, and a magician, a use it calls out of date. The Dial takes the last. A chapter earlier it writes *Magi* for the same word.
To dispense someone from a thing, in Littré, is to permit him not to do what is commanded, as to let him off a fast. *Free* keeps the freedom and drops the permission.
*Sol* is the ground and, in particular, Littré says, the top layer of farmland. The paragraph ends on *Paysan*, a man of the country.
Littré defines *devoir*, duty, as what law or morality obliges one to do, and *morale* as the rules that show a man his duties. *A job* answers neither.
*Dois* is must. The noun *devoir* is the infinitive of this verb. The Dial has *am going to*, and the obligation is gone.
*Rugueuse* is said of a rough surface and comes from the Latin for a wrinkle. *Étreindre* is to bind or squeeze tight. A French proverb sets it against *embrasser*, to take in one’s arms.
The French says carried off. A familiar French oath, Littré notes, has the devil do the carrying, and the Dial writes him in.
Two words, a sentence to themselves, in the form for *we*: let us go. The Dial joins them to the sentence before and keeps to *I*. In “Bad Blood” it renders the same word *Come!*

lenses.caption: Three of the Dial’s choices change what the French says. Dispensé, permitted not to do what is commanded, becomes free. Devoir, duty, becomes a job, and je dois, I must, becomes I am going to. Littré defines a duty as what law or morality obliges one to do. So the French excuses him from morality and gives him a duty to look for; in the Dial that pair is gone. Mage is in Littré a priest of ancient Persia, one of the three Magi, or, in a use it calls out of date, a magician; the Dial has a wizard. The English Auden quotes keeps the magus and the duty.
lenses.why: Where the French excuses him from morality and then hands him a duty, words Littré defines by each other, the Dial has free and a job; the pair is lost there, and kept in the English Auden quotes.
lenses.stands: The two passages side by side. Littré’s *Dictionnaire* under *mage*, *dispenser*, *devoir*, *morale*, *sol*, *paysan*, *rugueux*, *étreindre*, *embrasser*, *emporter* and *aller*. The Dial’s English of [“Morning”](#/read/rimbaud/s8:2) and of [“Bad Blood”](#/read/rimbaud/s2:22). The English Auden quotes: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 149–50.

auden.says: Auden’s two figures come from earlier in his chapter. Don Quixote is for him literature’s greatest picture of the religious hero, a man committed to something with absolute passion and forgetful of himself. Ishmael is the outcast son of Abraham in Genesis, whose name Melville gave to the teller of *Moby-Dick*; for Auden he is self-conscious, and a wanderer having no fixed commitment. Auden then quotes, in another English version, the last two paragraphs shown under “Adieu.” Artists of his own day, he adds, can neither have such heroic importance nor want it; reading the logs of the Romantics’ voyages, they should remember the voyagers’ courage.
auden.quote: the artist is not, as he had thought, Don Quixote, the Religious Hero, but only Ishmael, the explorer of possibility
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), chapter 3, pp. 94, 96–97, 100–102 and 149–50

auden.says: Before quoting Rimbaud, Auden describes the Romantic artist. Earlier artists, he says, recorded what other men did and thought; the Romantic artist is himself the epic hero, and the deeds he sets down are his own. From about 1770 to 1914 the heroes of the age are individual geniuses and not men of action, and what an artist can learn he learns mostly from himself. He is a *poète maudit*, a poet under a curse: a disaster has singled him out and gives him the passion to go on. Auden asks whether a longing for innocence does not belong to a life spent exploring the unknown and unconscious.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), chapter 3, pp. 147–48

auden.says: Auden’s sonnet “Rimbaud” gives the life in fourteen lines. Cold made the child a poet; drink, paid for by a weaker poet, disordered his senses and rid him of the nonsense he had grown up with, until he turned from poetry and from weakness alike. Verse had come to seem a sickness of the ear. The sonnet leaves him riding through Africa and dreaming of another self, an engineer with a son, whose truth liars could accept.
auden.source: “Rimbaud,” in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945), pp. 121–22

auden.says: In *New Year Letter*, published in 1941, the year of the course, Auden pictures the tribunal before which each poet must answer for his work; each may choose whom he faces. Three sit on Auden’s bench. The one presiding was taken through the three realms of the dead: Dante’s journey. William Blake sits on his right. On his left sits the young Rimbaud, frowning, an adolescent whom the poem calls quick and intolerant and credits with killing off an old rhetoric. He mutters a phrase from “Bad Blood”: *terror is not French*. Auden’s notes to the poem give that passage in French.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (1941), Part I, in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945), pp. 269–70, and his note to line 195

auden.says: Reviewing a life of Rimbaud in 1939, Auden judged that Rimbaud the man of action failed and tormented himself, because the will alone is not enough to live by. In 1947, writing on Baudelaire, he found no real change of heart in Rimbaud’s turn from poet to trader: to him the trader was the old dandy in a new form, as proud as before and as bent on being unlike everyone else.
auden.source: “Heretics” (1939) and the introduction to Baudelaire’s *Intimate Journals* (1947), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 32 and 314–15

auden.says: In his inaugural lecture at Oxford in 1956 Auden speaks of the Rimbaud Myth: the story that a great poet gave up writing because he chose to and not, as Coleridge did, because he had run out of things to say. He is fairly sure the story is not true. As a myth, he says, it weighs on the conscience of artists in his century. He brings it up while saying that a poet’s wish to find a justification for writing verse in the first place has lately grown stronger.
auden.source: “Making, Knowing and Judging” (1956), in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 53–54

auden.says: Writing on Marianne Moore, Auden says that an English ear can hardly take in verse measured by nothing but the count of its syllables. His case is the French twelve-syllable line: the English ear, he says, hears most such lines as anapests, two light syllables and a stress, a measure that in English goes with light verse.

sources: The French text: Arthur Rimbaud, *Une saison en enfer* (Brussels: Alliance typographique, 1873), as Project Gutenberg gives it (no. 56668). The two chapters were compared with the first edition as shown on French Wikisource.
The English: “A Season in Hell,” *The Dial* (New York), July 1920, pp. 1–26, unsigned and attributed to J. S. Watson, Jr. The translator’s note is on pp. 1–2.

W. H. Auden, *The Enchafèd Flood, or The Romantic Iconography of the Sea* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967): chapter 3, “Ishmael–Don Quixote,” pp. 94, 96–97, 100–102 and 146–50. The lectures were given at the University of Virginia in March 1949.

W. H. Auden, “Rimbaud” and *New Year Letter*, Part I, in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (New York: Random House, 1945), pp. 121–22 and 269–70. His note to line 195 of *New Year Letter* (1941): not seen.

W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “Making, Knowing and Judging” (1956), pp. 53–54, and “Marianne Moore,” p. 297.

Émile Littré, *Dictionnaire de la langue française* (Paris, 1863–77), at littre.org, under: hallucination, franchement, sophisme, magique, sacré, désordre, oisif, salon, calèche, vaudeville, épouvante, félicité, bête, chenille, représenter, limbes, taupe, vieillerie, étude, saluer, expression, bouffon, égaré, égarement, possible, retrouver, éternité, mêlé, mage, dispenser, rendu, sol, devoir, morale, paysan, rugueux, étreindre, embrasser, emporter, aller, maudit, asyndète, disjonction and anaphore.

Noël and Chapsal, *Nouvelle grammaire française*, revised by A. Vaillant (Philadelphia: Moss, 1863), nos. 118 and 479 to 481 (pp. 31–32 and 146–47): the past tenses; nos. 670 to 672 (p. 203): the colon.
L. E. Kastner, *A History of French Versification* (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1903): chapter 1 (pp. 1–2), chapter 2 (pp. 4–5), chapter 3 (p. 39) and chapter 8 (pp. 151–52).
Arthur Rimbaud, “Éternité,” in *Les Illuminations* (Paris: La Vogue, 1886), pp. 85–86, as shown on French Wikisource.
*Encyclopaedia Britannica*, eleventh edition (1911), vol. 23, “Rimbaud, Jean Arthur”: his dates.

The reading list of Auden’s course, English 135 (University of Michigan, 1941), in the image posted by Alan Jacobs, “Auden’s Syllabus” (blog.ayjay.org, 2012): it names the book as *Une Saison en Enfer*, “tr. Schwartz,” New Directions.
caveats: Auden set this book for his class in a translation by Schwartz, published by New Directions, which is in copyright. The English printed here is the unsigned version from *The Dial* of 1920. The English Auden quotes in 1949 is not the Dial’s.

No record was found of what Auden said about Rimbaud in the 1941 class. The view given here comes from lectures of 1949, printed as *The Enchafèd Flood*; the page numbers are those of the Vintage Books edition of 1967.

Three things given here as Auden’s were not seen in full copies of his text: the review “Heretics” (1939), the introduction to Baudelaire’s *Intimate Journals* (1947) and his note to line 195 of *New Year Letter*.
In this book the last line of the stanza has three syllables; printed on its own in 1886 it has five. It is not known whether Rimbaud shortened it on purpose or wrote the poem down from memory.

The stress marked on *Quoi?* is one reader’s hearing. In the first passage the form *finis* could also be a present tense; it is read as a past, as the Dial reads it. The third passage leaves out the short sixth paragraph of “Adieu,” as Auden’s quotation does.
